Cardiovascular Disease

Acute Heart Failure

Acute heart failure is not one disease. In the ED it is a phenotype problem: hypertensive pulmonary edema, normotensive congestion, acute-on-chronic decompensation, right-heart failure, high-output failure, or cardiogenic shock.

Board trap: do not let BNP replace bedside probability. Use history, exam, ECG/CXR, renal context, ultrasound, and response to therapy together.

Tintinalli Table 53-1 separates the clinical presentations that drive therapy. Hypertensive AHF is afterload-sensitive and nitrate/NIPPV responsive; pulmonary edema is primarily respiratory distress; cardiogenic shock is hypotension with tissue hypoperfusion; acute-on-chronic HF may be gradual and volume-overloaded; high-output HF is warm and tachycardic; right HF is low-output with JVD/hepatomegaly. Precipitants in Table 53-2 should be actively sought because many are reversible in the ED.

Diagnosis and Biomarkers

There is no single diagnostic test for acute heart failure. Orthopnea, PND, dyspnea at rest, prior HF, S3, JVD, edema, ischemic ECG change, CXR edema, and natriuretic peptides all move probability but none stands alone. Chest radiography can show venous congestion, cardiomegaly, and interstitial/alveolar edema, but may be negative early or in chronic compensated congestion.

BNP and NT-proBNP are best used when the ED diagnosis remains uncertain after the first bedside pass. Low values help rule out HF, high values support HF, and middle-range values require context. Older age, renal dysfunction, obesity, atrial fibrillation, and ARNI therapy can shift interpretation.

POCUS Pattern

Lung ultrasound asks whether the dyspneic patient has pulmonary congestion. Multiple bilateral B-lines support interstitial edema, but B-lines can also appear with pneumonia, fibrosis, contusion, or ARDS. The Tintinalli pathway then adds IVC size/collapsibility, evidence of acute RV strain, and estimated LVEF to sort AHF likely vs alternative diagnoses and HFrEF vs HFpEF.

Use POCUS to speed a clinical decision, not to avoid reassessment. If oxygenation, work of breathing, or blood pressure deteriorates, treatment should proceed while the diagnostic frame is refined.

Initial Treatment

Start with oxygen only when needed, target saturation at least 95% in typical AHF, and use NIPPV early for severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema, or impending fatigue. Intubate if mental status, shock, refractory hypoxemia, or inability to tolerate noninvasive ventilation makes it necessary.

Hypertensive AHF is treated by rapid afterload/preload reduction. Tintinalli Table 53-4 emphasizes sublingual nitroglycerin, NIPPV or intubation when severe, IV nitroglycerin for persistent hypertension/distress, then loop diuretic if there is volume overload. If hypotension follows vasodilators, Table 53-5 forces a search for excessive vasodilation, occult preload dependence, RV infarction, cardiogenic shock/MI, aortic stenosis, anaphylaxis, or sepsis.

For normotensive congested AHF, loop diuretics relieve congestion. Table 53-6 gives practical ED doses: furosemide 20-40 mg IV if diuretic naive; if already on oral loop therapy, use roughly 1 to 2.5 times the total daily oral furosemide-equivalent dose as IV. Bumetanide and torsemide are alternatives. Reassess urine output, dyspnea, renal function, potassium, magnesium, and blood pressure.

Low Output and Shock

AHF with hypotension, altered mentation, cool extremities, oliguria, rising lactate, ischemic symptoms, or poor perfusion is a different patient than uncomplicated congestion. Treat as cardiogenic shock until proven otherwise: monitor closely, obtain ECG/troponin, look for STEMI or mechanical complications, and involve cardiology/critical care early.

Rosen separates stabilization from definitive management. Norepinephrine is commonly first-line for hypotensive shock; small fluid boluses are only for selected preload-responsive patients; dobutamine, epinephrine, milrinone, or mechanical support may be needed depending on the hemodynamic problem. If STEMI is present, disposition must center on PCI-capable care.

Disposition

Disposition is based on more than symptom improvement. Tintinalli Figure 53-3 frames three axes: clinical gestalt, physiologic risk, and self-care capacity. Table 53-7 shows why risk tools are imperfect: different studies use different predictors, but renal dysfunction, sodium, blood pressure, troponin/BNP, respiratory rate, oxygenation, RR, comorbidities, and functional status recur.

Observation or short-stay care is reasonable only when the patient improves and lacks exclusion criteria. Table 53-8 recommends excluding positive troponin, BUN >40, creatinine >3, sodium <135, ischemic ECG changes, new-onset AHF, active IV vasoactive infusion, major comorbidity needing acute intervention, RR ≥32 or NIPPV requirement at observation consideration, poor perfusion, poor social support, or poor follow-up.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. Acute heart failure is best framed in the ED as:

A. A BNP diagnosis onlyBiomarkers support but do not define the entire syndrome.
B. A syndrome of elevated filling pressure or low output with phenotype-directed treatmentCorrect.
C. Always isolated renal failureRenal disease may precipitate or complicate AHF.
D. Always pneumoniaPneumonia is an important mimic/precipitant.

Q2. Tintinalli's AHF phenotypes include:

A. Hypertensive AHF, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, acute-on-chronic HF, high-output HF, and right HFCorrect.
B. Only STEMIACS can precipitate AHF but is not the only phenotype.
C. Only vasovagal syncopeNo.
D. Only COPDCOPD is a mimic and comorbidity.

Q3. Common precipitants of AHF include:

A. Medication adherence onlyNonadherence is common but incomplete.
B. Only viral URIInfection may contribute, but this misses the core list.
C. Nonadherence, renal failure, substance abuse, hypertension, iatrogenic fluid/drugs, and dysrhythmiaCorrect.
D. Only hypoglycemiaNo.

Q4. The single diagnostic test that rules in acute HF in all ED patients is:

A. BNPBNP helps most when pretest probability is intermediate.
B. Chest radiographCXR can be falsely negative.
C. ECGECG finds precipitants but is not definitive.
D. NoneCorrect.

Q5. BNP/NT-proBNP is most useful when:

A. Clinical uncertainty remains after history, exam, ECG, and CXRCorrect.
B. The diagnosis is already obviousLess useful when the bedside diagnosis is already clear.
C. It replaces physician assessmentNo.
D. It is interpreted without age or renal contextRenal function, age, obesity, and ARNI therapy matter.

Q6. A low BNP value is strongest for:

A. Ruling in HFHigh values rule in better.
B. Ruling out HF when below the low cut pointCorrect.
C. Diagnosing PENo.
D. Diagnosing sepsisNo.

Q7. In lung ultrasound for AHF, B-lines represent:

A. Pneumothorax onlyPneumothorax lacks lung sliding and B-lines.
B. Free air under diaphragmNo.
C. Thickened interlobular septa/interstitial pulmonary edema patternCorrect.
D. Normal lung sliding onlyNot enough.

Q8. Tintinalli's bedside US pathway asks all except:

A. Are there pulmonary congestion signs?Part of the pathway.
B. Is IVC size/collapsibility consistent with overload?Part of the pathway.
C. Is LVEF reduced or preserved?Part of the pathway.
D. Is serum amylase elevated?Correct; not part of the AHF US pathway.

Q9. Hypertensive AHF treatment starts with:

A. Oxygen if needed, sublingual nitroglycerin, NIPPV/intubation if severe, then IV nitroglycerin when indicatedCorrect.
B. Large crystalloid bolus for everyoneFluid overload is common; indiscriminate bolus can worsen AHF.
C. Morphine as the primary therapyMorphine is not preferred.
D. Routine beta-blocker loadingNot initial ED therapy for most.

Q10. In hypertensive AHF, nitrates mainly help by:

A. Increasing afterloadOpposite.
B. Reducing preload and at higher doses afterloadCorrect.
C. Blocking infectionNo.
D. Increasing bronchospasmNo.

Q11. After vasodilator-associated hypotension, think of:

A. Only anxietyNo.
B. Only painNo.
C. Excessive vasodilation, HOCM, intravascular depletion, RV infarction, cardiogenic shock/MI, aortic stenosis, anaphylaxis, or sepsisCorrect.
D. Only medication tasteNo.

Q12. Normotensive congested AHF is commonly treated first with:

A. Immediate thrombolysis for allOnly if another diagnosis requires it.
B. No oxygen everOxygen is used when hypoxemic.
C. Only antibioticsAntibiotics if infection is suspected.
D. Loop diuretics with reassessment of urine output and symptomsCorrect.

Q13. A loop-diuretic naive patient may receive:

A. Furosemide 20-40 mg IV pushCorrect.
B. Nitroprusside 10 mg/kg bolusWrong dose/drug context.
C. Warfarin loading for everyoneNo.
D. No reassessmentReassessment is essential.

Q14. For a patient already on oral furosemide, a reasonable initial IV dose is:

A. Always 1 mgToo low for many.
B. About 1-2.5 times the oral furosemide dose as IV furosemide equivalentCorrect.
C. Always 500 mgExcessive for most.
D. Never diuresisWrong.

A. Avoiding all diureticsNo.
B. Only oral therapyNo.
C. Higher initial IV dosing may produce faster symptom improvement but requires renal monitoringCorrect.
D. Nitrates are never usedFalse.

B. Clearly mortality-improvingNo.
C. Required before nitratesNo.

B. Low-risk dischargeUnsafe.

C. Discharge before treatmentUnsafe.

Q19. Cardiogenic shock due to STEMI in AHF generally requires:

A. Only PO fluidsNo.

D. No consultationUnsafe.

Q20. Disposition decisions in AHF should include:

A. Clinical gestaltTrue.
B. Physiologic risk profileTrue.

Q21. Heart failure observation unit exclusion criteria include:

A. Positive troponin, BUN >40, creatinine >3, sodium <135, ischemic ECG change, new AHF onset, active IV vasoactives, significant comorbidity, high RR/NIPPV, poor perfusion, poor support/follow-upCorrect.
B. Normal renal function onlyNot an exclusion.
C. Good follow-up onlyNot an exclusion.
D. Resolved symptoms onlyNot an exclusion alone.

Q22. Table 53-7 risk-stratification studies show:

A. No variables matterWrong.
B. Variables differ, but renal dysfunction, BP, troponin/BNP, sodium, RR, oxygenation, and comorbidities recurCorrect.
C. All patients are low riskFalse.
D. Disposition is never uncertainFalse.

Q23. A patient with AHF and new ischemic ECG changes should:

A. Go to short-stay unit automaticallyUnsafe.
B. Be discharged if BNP improvesUnsafe.
C. Be evaluated for ACS/high-risk admission pathwayCorrect.
D. Receive no troponinWrong.

Q24. Rosen Table 67.2 reinforces that among binary tests, strong AHF diagnostic support can come from:

A. POCUS B-linesTrue.
B. Interstitial/alveolar edema on CXRTrue.
C. High natriuretic peptide thresholdsTrue.
D. All of these, interpreted with pretest probabilityCorrect.

Q25. The safest ED summary statement is:

A. Treat the phenotype, reassess oxygenation/BP/urine output, and disposition by risk plus self-care capacityCorrect.
B. BNP alone determines dischargeNo.
C. All AHF patients need morphineNo.
D. All AHF patients can leave after diuresisNo.

Q26. Which finding pushes away from low-risk discharge?

A. Symptoms resolved, no high-risk features, reliable follow-upLower risk.
B. Cardiogenic shock or respiratory failureCorrect.
C. Stable BP and improving dyspneaLower risk.
D. Prescribed and adherent GDMTSupports outpatient safety when otherwise low risk.
